content: Leishmaniasis is a disease caused by a parasite. This parasite is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected sand flies. There are two primary forms of leishmaniasis: cutaneous leishmaniasis and visceral leishmaniasis. The most common symptom of cutaneous leishmaniasis is the development of skin sores. These sores can vary in size and appearance over time. They may present as closed lesions, resembling lumps or bumps, or as open ulcers. Some individuals may also experience swollen lymph nodes near the affected areas. Visceral leishmaniasis, on the other hand, is characterized by systemic symptoms such as fever and weight loss. Patients with this form of the disease may also develop an enlarged spleen (splenomegaly) and liver (hepatomegaly). Additionally, they may exhibit low red blood cell counts (anemia), low white blood cell counts (leukopenia), and low platelet counts (thrombocytopenia). It is important to note that some individuals infected with leishmaniasis may remain asymptomatic and never develop noticeable symptoms. Sand flies, the vectors of leishmaniasis, are found in specific regions, including parts of Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Southern Europe, Mexico, Central America, and South America. Travelers visiting these areas are at risk of being bitten by sand flies and potentially contracting the disease. Currently, there is no vaccine or medication available to prevent leishmaniasis. To reduce the risk of infection, travelers are advised to use EPA-registered insect repellents containing active ingredients such as DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE). These repellents are safe and effective when used as directed, even for pregnant and breastfeeding women. If sunscreen is also being used, insect repellent should be applied after sunscreen. For infants and children, additional precautions should be taken. Dress them in clothing that covers their arms and legs, and use mosquito netting to cover strollers and baby carriers. When applying insect repellent to children, follow label instructions carefully. Avoid using products containing OLE or para-menthane-diol (PMD) on children under three years old. Do not apply repellent to a child’s hands, eyes, mouth, or irritated skin. Adults should spray repellent onto their hands first and then apply it to a child’s face. Permethrin, an insecticide that kills or repels insects such as mosquitoes and sand flies, can be used to treat clothing and gear, including boots, pants, socks, and tents. Permethrin-treated clothing provides protection even after multiple washes. Always follow product instructions when treating items yourself, and never apply permethrin directly to the skin. To further protect against sand flies and mosquitoes, choose accommodations with air conditioning or screened windows and doors. If staying in a location without these features or sleeping outdoors, use a mosquito net. Opt for a compact, white, rectangular mosquito net with 156 holes per square inch, long enough to tuck under the mattress. Permethrin-treated mosquito nets offer additional protection compared to untreated ones. Follow label instructions to determine if a treated net can be washed. If bitten by mosquitoes or sand flies, avoid scratching the bites. To relieve itching, apply over-the-counter anti-itch or antihistamine creams.
